paper_title: The Router Within: Eliciting Native Skill Routing from a Frozen LLM

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Skills extend an LLM agent beyond its parametric knowledge, and the gain they promise rests on picking the right one. Deployed harnesses route by preloading every skill's metadata into the context, which disperses the agent's attention and caps the library size. Retrieval pipelines move the selection out of the context, but also out of the agent's capability. We show that the frozen agent LLM already carries the routing signal in its own forward passes, and that two linear maps suffice to read it out with no skill text in the context. Gavel (Glance And Verdict from a frozen LLM) reads it in two steps. A glance projects the task's and each skill's mid-layer states through the two maps, the only parameters trained, and scores the full library against compact per-skill banks that one forward pass builds at installation. A verdict then resumes the shortlisted skills' forward passes and reads the model's own likelihood and yes/no judgment, fused with the glance as a product of experts. Trained once, Gavel transfers zero-shot to three public benchmarks and SkillTraj, our new benchmark of 372 simulated agent trajectories. On Qwen3-32B it outperforms progressive disclosure and retrieve-and-rerank pipelines that add 1.2B to 16B external parameters, by up to 13.4 points on written tasks and up to 21.9 when the need for a skill arises mid-rollout. Routing accuracy improves as the backbone does, and in a bash-agent harness the same 32B triggers the correct skill on Skill-Use more often than far larger frontier models running in Codex.

Introduction Skills have become the standard way to extend an LLM agent beyond its parametric knowledge (Anthropic, 2025; Xu & Yan, 2026). skill packages instructions, scripts, and reference files in SKILL.md document that the agent loads into its context when task calls for it. well-chosen skill improves task performance, while an ill-suited one leaves it worse off than no skill at all (Li et al., 2026), and the choice grows harder as public libraries reach tens of thousands of entries (OpenAI, 2026a; Gao et al., 2026). Selecting the right skill from such library is therefore the central problem, and current systems take one of two routes. Deployed agents, Claude Code and Codex among them, route by progressive disclosure (Anthropic, 2025; OpenAI, 2026a): they preload every installed skills name and description into the system prompt and let the agent LLM itself decide which to read in full. The metadata, however, crowds the context in proportion to the library, degrading the agents work on the task (Liu et al., 2024; Modarressi et al., 2025). Codex therefore caps skill metadata at 2% of the context window and drops the rest (OpenAI, 2026a), confining deployment to small library, where routing accuracy still decays logarithmically with the number of skills (Chen et al., 2026a). The cost is intrinsic, since routing inside the context spreads the agents attention thin over every skill it considers and weighs

sections.content: Figure 1 Three designs for skill routing. (a) Progressive disclosure preloads every skills metadata into the prompt, crowding the context. (b) Retrieve-and-rerank keeps the context clean but hands selection to external models that never see the rollout. (c) Gavel routes with the frozen agent LLM itself: glance over the whole library, read from one mid-layer state through two trained linear maps, then verdict in which the same model examines the top candidates in full. only the summaries that fit, which omit much of what selection depends on (Zheng et al., 2026). To lift this burden from the context, recent skill routers, following tool learning (Qin et al., 2024a; Zheng et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026), hand the selection to external models. retrieval pipeline, usually an embedding model and reranker, picks skills and injects them into the context. The context is relieved, but the selection is also cut off from the agents capability. standalone retriever may excel at matching text, but judges what task needs less reliably than the agent LLM (Shi et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026), especially amid the noisy context where the need arises mid-rollout (Lumer et al., 2025; Fei et al., 2025), and it does not improve as the agent itself does. Selection inside the context thus taxes the agent, yet an external model does not understand tasks and skills as well as the agent does. Can router, then, select with the agents capability but outside its context? The open question is through what interface, and at what cost, that understanding can be turned to routing. We propose Gavel (Glance And Verdict from frozen LLM), the third design in Figure 1, which draws every routing signal from the frozen agent LLMs own forward passes through only two linear projections, and lets no skill text into the context until skill is chosen. Gavel routes in two stages, glance over the whole library followed by verdict on its shortlist. As the LLM decodes, its intermediate layers compress the inputs semantics (Skean et al., 2025), but entangle them with much that serves only the next token (Queipo-de Llano et al., 2026), so no native read-out ranks librarys skills (Appendix A). The glance therefore grafts new attention head onto the model. query map reads each task tokens state at mid layer, key map each skill tokens state at the same layer at installation, both trained contrastively so that task tokens strongest match lands on skill that serves it. Each task token votes for the skills it matches best, so its few decisive tokens are not averaged away. new skill thus costs one forward pass and no training. factorized head, however, misses subtler inferences routing can turn on. Full attention over skill and task together does not, but it costs one forward pass per candidate, which no library affords, so the verdict spends it on the glances shortlist alone. For each it resumes the installation pass with the task appended and reads from that forward how strongly the skill primes the model for the task, and its log-odds judgment of whether the skill serves it. We instantiate Gavel with Qwen3-32B as the agent LLM and train its two projections, 7.9M parameters in all, once on the synthetic queryskill pairs of SkillRet (Kang et al., 2026). We then evaluate it on three public skill-selection benchmarks, which depart from that corpus in query author, document genre, and library scale. All three hand the router written task, whereas live agents need often surfaces mid-rollout, so we also build SkillTraj, benchmark of 372 simulated agent trajectories that scores each router at that moment under four scenarios of noisy multi-turn context. Across all four, Gavel outperforms both progressive disclosure given well-chosen shortlist of twenty skills and retrieve-and-rerank pipelines that add 1.2B to 16B external parameters, by 13.4 points over the strongest pipeline on SRA-Bench and by 8.6 to 21.9 points across SkillTrajs four scenarios. Ablations isolate what each stage contributes, and routing improves as the backbone does. In minimal bash-agent harness, Qwen3-32B triggers the correct skill on Skill-Use (Han et al., 2026) more reliably than far larger open frontier models in Claude Code and Codex. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We propose Gavel (Glance And Verdict from frozen LLM), skill router that elicits routing from the frozen agent LLMs own forward passes and thus improves as the agent does, with no model beside it and no skill text in the context until one is chosen. On the technical side, token-level glance reads mid layer through two linear maps against skill banks thinned to 𝜀-covers with bounded distortion, and verdict reads generative and discriminative evidence from resumed forward pass, fused as product of experts. We build SkillTraj, benchmark of 372 simulated agent trajectories that scores router at the moment skill becomes needed, under four scenarios of noisy multi-turn context. Across three public benchmarks and SkillTraj, Gavel outperforms progressive disclosure and retrieve-and-rerank pipelines that add up to 16B external parameters, by up to 21.9 points, and in live harness has Qwen3-32B load the correct skill more often than far larger frontier models. 2. Related Work Skill and tool selection. Deployed harnesses route by progressive disclosure, holding every skills metadata in context for the agent to read (Anthropic, 2025; OpenAI, 2026a). Retrieval-based systems move the selection to an external stack, built over API pools (Qin et al., 2024a; Lumer et al., 2025), invoked mid-rollout (Fei et al., 2025), or trained on full skill documents (Zheng et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). ToolkenGPT (Hao et al., 2023) has frozen LLM emit tool as token, but trains one embedding per tool, so new tool costs training run. Gavel instead draws the routing signal from the agents own forward passes, with no skill text in the context and no model beside the backbone. Reading information out of an LLM. Probing shows that hidden states carry more than the next token needs (Alain & Bengio, 2017; Belinkov, 2022). Text-embedding work scales this read-out, turning decoder LLMs into strong encoders by fine-tuning (Wang et al., 2024; BehnamGhader et al., 2024) or by prompting alone (Springer et al., 2025). GRIT (Muennighoff et al., 2025) unifies embedding and generation in one model, but fine-tunes the whole backbone. The predictions are just as readable, and rerankers score document by the likelihood it assigns to the query (Sachan et al., 2022; Zhuang et al., 2023) or by the models own yes/no relevance judgment (Nogueira et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2023). Gavel turns these read-outs into skill router on the frozen agent LLM itself.

sections.content: 3. Gavel: Routing on the Agents Own Forward Passes 3.1. Problem setup and design principles We model skill routing as follows. skill library = {𝑠1, . . . , 𝑠𝑁 } is set of documents, each metadata header (name and description) followed by body of instructions. The agent is frozen LLM decoding rollout. At routing point, its context 𝑥 holds the task, either user request or an execution state reached mid-rollout. router observes 𝑥 and and decides which skill to load. Current practice, as Section 1 reviewed it, gives rise to three requirements on router. (i) Task-only context. Skill metadata preloaded into the prompt disperses the agents attention and hurts its work on the task (Liu et al., 2024; Modarressi et al., 2025), so no skill text may enter the context until one is chosen. (ii) No standalone model. The agent LLM judges tasks needs more reliably than standalone retriever (Shi et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026), so selection should inherit that capability and improve as the agent does, with anything added on top lightweight. (iii) Installation-time indexing. Skills are files dropped in folder, and public libraries hold tens of thousands that keep changing (Gao et al., 2026), so no training may be run for new skill. Gavel satisfies all three (Figure 2). The glance (Sections 3.2 and 3.3) ranks the full library by matching hidden states of on the task against those that single forward pass extracts per skill at installation, with no training run. The verdict (Section 3.4) re-examines the shortlist with few forward passes of over skill and task together, and Section 3.5 fuses their three read-outs as product of experts. Throughout, ℎℓ (𝑐) denotes the layer-ℓ hidden states of on input 𝑐. 3.2. We therefore rule by the product of experts (Hinton, 2002), 𝑆(𝑠𝑥) = 𝑔(𝑠𝑥) + 𝛼 𝐿(𝑠𝑥) + 𝛾 𝑉 (𝑠𝑥), (6) so that 𝑒𝑆 multiplies the three experts, and any one of them can veto candidate the other two merely tolerate. The coefficients are exchange rates that convert the nats of the likelihood and the judgment onto the glances scale, and tempering exponents that discount an overconfident expert. Gavel loads the skill whose 𝑆 is highest among the candidates the glance shortlisted. 4. Experiments 4.1. Setup Our main experiments run Gavel on Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025) as the frozen agent backbone, where the matrix-entropy criterion of Section 3.2 places the read-out after block 45 of the models 64 (Appendix B). The projections 𝑊𝑞 and 𝑊𝑠, with 7.9M parameters in total, are trained once, at temperature 𝜏 = 40, on 51,104 of SkillRets training queries (Kang et al., 2026), written by Qwen3.5 over 9,084 skills collected from public repositories. The cover radius 𝜀 = 0.83 is fixed on the same split, and shrinks the skill banks about 8.5 at cost of at most 1.6 points on any benchmark below. The exchange rates (𝛼, 𝛾) = (1.0, 0.025) and the pruning margin Δ = 0.133 are calibrated on SkillRets validation split, and only the candidates the glance scores within Δ of its best, roughly nine on average, receive verdict. With the projections and these four scalars held fixed, every number on every other library is zero-shot. Appendix rebuilds the pipeline on Gemma backbone and repeats the main comparison. Appendix collects further ablations. 4.2. Routing from written tasks We first evaluate routing from written tasks on three benchmarks. SkillRets official test set (v1) pairs 4,997 Claude-written queries with library of 6,660 held-out skills. SRA-Bench (Su et al., 2026) changes the genre on both sides, with tasks from six reasoning and coding benchmarks and 26,262 skills, most collected from the web. It ships no test split, so we evaluate stratified sample of 861 tasks. Eval-Core, SkillRouters own benchmark adapted from SkillsBench (Li et al., 2026), poses 75 real task.md queries against 78K documents in two pools (Zheng et al., 2026). router is scored by whether the single skill it commits to serves the task, Hit@1 over the full library. On all three benchmarks gold labels miss adequate skills, as exhaustive annotation is impractical. We therefore score Hit@1 by adjudication. GPT-5.6 Sol (high) (OpenAI, 2026c) compares the committed skill with every gold in both orders, given only the task and both documents. The skill is credited when it wins at least as often as it loses across all golds. Appendix gives examples of under-annotated queries, the unadjudicated scores, and human check of the verdicts.

sections.title: 4.2.1 Comparison with current practice
sections.content: Gavel is compared against the best of current practice. Progressive disclosure cannot survey thousands of skills in context, so we give it retrieval front end. Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025), the top open embedding model on MTEB, shortlists twenty skills for the agent to pick from. Retrieveand-rerank comes in the form SkillRouter ships, 0.6B embedder and 0.6B reranker trained for

sections.content: skill selection (Zheng et al., 2026), and in scaled-up general-purpose form, Qwen3-Embedding8B followed by Qwen3-Reranker-8B. Alongside them we keep BM25 as the lexical anchor, and SKILLRET-Emb-0.6B, trained on SkillRet by its authors (Kang et al., 2026). As shown in Figure 3, Gavel leads all three benchmarks at both stages. The full pipeline beats the strongest pipeline by 3.8 points on SkillRet, 13.4 on SRA-Bench, and 1.3 to 2.7 on Eval-Core, and the glance alone is the strongest retrieval stage on SRA-Bench and Eval-Core while coming within point of the best embedder on SkillRet (candidate-pool recall tells much the same story, Appendix H.3). The two trained embedders, SKILLRET-Emb-0.6B and SkillRouters, match the glance on SkillRet, whose queries and skills resemble their training data. However, once the query style shifts from conversational user requests to the task.md project files of Eval-Core, both begin to lag, and when the skills shift as well, from SKILL.md files written for agents to the procedural web pages of SRA-Bench, both fall below even BM25, the out-of-domain failure dense retrievers are known for (Thakur et al., 2021). Figure 3 Routing from written tasks. Light fill is the retrieval stage committing its top-1 alone, dark fill the full pipeline built on it, and on Eval-Core the hatched bar is the hard pool. Where BM25 falls below the plotted range its score is printed in place of the bar. The untrained Qwen3-Embedding-8B exhibits the opposite preference. On Eval-Core and SRA-Bench, matching task file against skill document is close to the web-scale retrieval it was trained for, and it fares well. SkillRets conversational requests share little vocabulary with the skill body (Shi et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026), and there it trails even the far smaller trained embedders. Whether the shortlist is then handed to progressive disclosure or to dedicated reranker, these widely practiced pipelines place an external model beside the agent, from 1.2B to 16B parameters against our 7.9M, but none of them closes the gap to router read out of the agent itself.

sections.content: Figure 4 Ablations. Each row replaces one design choice of Gavel and shows how far the full pipeline drops on each benchmark, in points against the unmodified router (red line). On Eval-Core the hollow marker is the easy pool and the filled one the hard pool. yet loses badly on every benchmark even with the verdict behind it. The glance profits from the far better compression of the agent LLM it reads, not from how the tokens are compared. Product of experts pointwise rerank. We restore the classical division of labor, retrieval only nominating and reranker alone deciding, by committing to 𝑉, the backbones judgment of each candidate on its own, and discarding 𝑔 and 𝐿. This runs into the poor calibration of self-reported judgment (Qin et al., 2024b), and on SkillRet it scrambles the ambiguous queries. Verdict skill body in generation. This variant appends the skill after the task, takes the mean log-likelihood of its body in place of the query-likelihood of Eq. (4), and reads 𝑉 with the same question. But bodys likelihood speaks more to how much the skill resembles the models own writing than to whether it serves the task, bias the query-likelihood shares across all skills, leaving their ordering intact. Indeed the calibration discards the document-likelihood outright, driving 𝛼 to zero, and on the remaining two signals the variant falls visibly behind on every benchmark. Verdict progressive disclosure. Handing the glances twenty candidates to the menu of progressive disclosure tests whether the verdict earns its forward passes over letting the agent read the shortlist itself. The menu comes closest on Eval-Core, whose curated skills carry descriptions that summarize them well. But it falls far behind on SRA-Bench, where telling the right skill apart takes the long procedural detail in its body, yet the pick rests on metadata that cannot hold it. This is the information loss Zheng et al. (2026) identify, which the verdict escapes by reading the full body. Placing the twenty full bodies in the menu itself does not close the gap either (Appendix F.1). 4.3. Routing mid-rollout The benchmarks above hand the router written task that states its need in single clean turn. live agent instead works from long multi-turn context, and the need may surface only as it works through the task. We therefore build SkillTraj, new skill-routing benchmark of simulated agent rollouts. Each of its 372 trajectories is multi-turn dialogue with tool calls, rendered in the backbones chat template, and marks the point at which skill from the held-out SkillRet library of 6,660 becomes needed; router is scored on the skill it commits to at that point. The points cover four scenarios, by where the need comes from: stated outright by the user (user request, 116), revealed by tool result (tool evidence, 106), created by the agents own written plan (agent plan, 105), or arising after the agent has read the wrong skill and must reroute with the misleading document still in context (wrong-skill recovery, 45). Each trajectory is written by GPT-5.

Figure 5 compares Gavel against each pipeline taken both ways and against progressive disclosure, constrained to decode menu index. Gavel leads every scenario, by 8.6 to 21.9 points over the strongest other system. Yet the larger models cannot iron the noise out either; in all four scenarios they are better served by the clean last message than by the full context that holds all the usable evidence. sections.title: Eliciting Native Skill Routing from a Frozen LLM
sections.content: 5. Conclusion We presented Gavel, router that returns skill selection to the agent LLM without placing anything in its context. The glance scores the full library from mid-layer read-out of the frozen backbone, the verdict re-scores the shortlist from the models own generative and discriminative predictions, and two linear projections are all that is trained. Across three public benchmarks and SkillTraj this native read-out outperforms progressive disclosure and retrieve-and-rerank pipelines that add up to 16B external parameters, and in live harness it has Qwen3-32B load the correct skill more often than far larger frontier models. The frozen backbone already carries the capability that skill selection requires, and learned read-out is enough to put it to work. Whether the same read-out also routes tools, memories, or MCP servers from an agents own forward passes is question we leave open.

sections.content: The organization of the appendix is as follows: Appendix A: We present three read-outs that lean further on the backbones native machinery, each of which fails, and describe how each failure informs the adopted design. Appendix B: We describe how the read-out layer ℓ is selected. Appendix C: We provide the training details of the two projections 𝑊𝑞 and 𝑊𝑠. Appendix D: We provide the 𝜀-cover compression procedure for the key banks and prove its guarantees on score distortion and bank size. Appendix E: We rebuild the full pipeline on Gemma backbone of comparable size to test the method beyond the Qwen family. Appendix F: We provide additional ablations, including progressive disclosure over full skill bodies (F.1), the removal of single verdict signal (F.2), and the replacement of the glance with an off-the-shelf embedder (F.3). Appendix G: We reproduce every prompt template used in the experiments verbatim. Appendix H: We provide benchmark details, including examples of under-annotated golds (H.1), raw scores and the agreement between the judge and human labels (H.2), the candidate-pool recall of every retrieval stage (H.3), and the construction of SkillTraj (H.4). Appendix I: We walk through transcripts from the Skill-Use rollouts. Appendix J: We analyze the cost of skill routing per session. Appendix K: We discuss the gate and routing behind cloud API.

sections.content: A. Native read-outs that fail The glance reads through two trained maps and aggregates the per-token scores under handcrafted decay 𝑤𝑖, rather than through machinery the model already owns. This appendix records three alternatives that lean further toward the native machinery. Each fails, and each failure fixes one piece of the adopted design. Native attention keys as the matching space. Attention already computes token-level querykey matches, so the most native glance would use them directly, indexing skill by the pre-rotary keys the backbones own heads assign to its tokens and matching the tasks native queries against that bank. Without training, the best of 24 configurations of head selection, low-rank whitening, and aggregation reaches Hit@1 .001 on the SkillRet validation library of 10,123 skills, against .918 for the trained glance head, and exact zeros on SRA-Bench, where even its recall at 20 falls below random ranking. Most of the loss comes from calibration, since native scores are not comparable across documents encoded in separate sequences. Restricted to 20-candidate shortlist, the same read-out scores .099, twice in-pool chance. Training mixer over per-head scores does not repair it. The mixture becomes usable shortlist reranker but drops 7.6 points when asked to rank the full library, and its weights are library-bound, losing 1.2 points on the library they were fitted on and 24 on another. Equal-weight and non-negative mixtures collapse further, which rules out negative weights as the cause. The native keys do carry real signal, one to two orders of magnitude too faint. The best single head reaches .084 alone, and the ranking of heads is stable across libraries, yet no priori criterion finds the good ones (the head placing the most attention mass on the gold document ranks 29th by retrieval). Trained projections are what turn this signal into usable one. Initializing from native heads. The trained head still needs an initialization and shape, and the native machinery might supply both, stacking the query and key maps of six strong native heads up to the glances dimension as the initialization of 𝑊𝑞 and 𝑊𝑠, or keeping six separate heads whose scores average. On the SkillRet validation library, native initialization ends 0.7 points below random initialization, the multi-head shape 0.6 points below the single wide head, and the two combined lose 4.6. Selecting which heads to stack contributes nothing either, as six randomly chosen heads beat the six the mixer above weights highest by 1.3 points. The glance head is therefore single map, randomly initialized. Trained retrieval tokens. The decay 𝑤𝑖 in the vote of Section 3.2 is the one hand-crafted piece of the glance, and native attention is the natural candidate to replace it: append 64 trained retrieval tokens to the context, let each aggregate the preceding tokens through the backbones own attention, pass their hidden states through 𝑊𝑞, and average their votes. Trained on the same corpus as the glance, the tokens learn recency read-out instead, settling their attention on the most recent stretch of context rather than allocating it by content. We attribute this more to the data than to the idea. The plentiful supervision consists of clean single-turn requests, where the recent context is the task and recency is sufficient policy, so nothing forces the tokens to allocate attention selectively, yet the router must survive contexts whose trigger sits buried mid-history. We therefore keep the hand-crafted decay, and leave learned aggregation, trained on data that rewards selectivity, to future work.

Your response must contain exactly ONE bash code block with ONE command (or commands connected with && or ). Explain your reasoning before your command. [the harnesss standard formatting example, rules, and command examples, unchanged from mini-sweagent] ## Available skills The following agent skills are installed. If skill applies to the task, read its SKILL.md first and follow it. - {name}: {description} Under this prompt the model reads skill on 2 of the 175 tasks that call for one. The listing itself serves the model well enough, since forcing its first action to read the one skill it picks from that listing raises the score to .834. The failure sits in the unprompted decision to consult skill at all. That decision is trained harness habit. Even the frontier models of Table 1, post-trained amid the skills ecosystem, swing by up to 38 points in trigger rate between the two harnesses the benchmark measures (Han et al., 2026), and Qwen3-32B predates that ecosystem altogether (Yang et al., 2025; Anthropic, 2025), so nothing in its training rewards pausing mid-task to read installed documentation. sections.title: Eliciting Native Skill Routing from a Frozen LLM
sections.content: the current state. skill carries roughly 100 tokens of metadata and 1,895-token body, the mean over 40,285 publicly listed skills (Ling et al., 2026); query carries 239 tokens, the mean over the SkillRet test set. Prices are GPT-5.6 Sols official rates2. Neither router decodes extra tokens, and both inject the chosen body after routing, so those costs cancel. Budgeting the injected bodies themselves is separate problem (Chen et al., 2026b). The gate and the glance read hidden states the rollout computes anyway, and the key bank is built offline once per library, so Gavel pays only for verdicts nine forwards per firing under the pruning margin of Section 4.1, each prefilling one candidates metadata and body followed by the query: 𝐶Gavel = 𝑚 9 (100 + 1,895 + 239) $4/106 $0.080 𝑚. The bill is independent of 𝑛 and 𝑇, and it is paid off-path: the forwards are batched prefills that never enter the rollouts context. Progressive disclosure keeps its 100𝑛-token metadata menu in the prompt prefix, and the serving API is stateless: every one of the 𝑇 calls re-sends the context, and all previous input tokens . . . are billed as input tokens each time (OpenAI, 2026b). The menu is therefore written to the prompt cache once and read back at the cached rate on the other 𝑇 1 calls: 𝐶PD = 100𝑛 (cid:0)$5 + $0.40 (𝑇 1)(cid:1)/106 $4 105 𝑛𝑇 . At realistic scales both bills are small and close: three firings cost $0.24, and hundred-skill menu over fifty calls costs $0.25. Which is smaller turns on 𝑚/𝑇 and 𝑛; Gavel is the cheaper router once 𝑛 exceeds roughly 2,000 𝑚/𝑇. Latency follows the same shape. The gate reads state the rollout has already computed, and the glance is one matrix multiply of the projected query tokens against the bank, milliseconds on GPU. The wait is the verdict: nine prefills of about 2.2K tokens each, batched in parallel, on the order of half second per firing on modern serving stack, and less once the per-skill prefixes are KV-cached. That pause is paid once per firing. Progressive disclosure adds no separate stage, but every decoded token of the session attends over the 100𝑛 menu positions; the prompt cache spares their recompute, and the attention scan over them stays on every step. The menus real cost is the window it occupies. It holds 100𝑛 tokens of the models finite context for the whole session, and metadata held in front of every call disperses the models attention and degrades its performance on the task itself (Liu et al., 2024; Modarressi et al., 2025). verdict forward never enters that window: the nine prefills run off-path, and their skill prefix is query-independent, so serving stack can cache it per skill and pay fresh input only for the live query. 2https://platform.openai.com/docs/pricing, August 2026: $4.00 per million input tokens, $0.40 per million cached reads, $5.00 per million cache writes. We ignore the long-context surcharge on requests beyond 272K input tokens.

sections.title: Eliciting Native Skill Routing from a Frozen LLM
sections.content: K. Discussion The gate. The gate of Section 4.4 is linear classifier over two read-outs the rollout already produces, the glance scores that the context has accumulated over the library and the final-layer state at the current position, and it fires once it stays on for two consecutive tokens. We trained it once on SkillTraj and did not engineer it further, since the question Section 4.4 asks is whether the routing signal survives live rollout, not how precisely call can be timed. Two designs would time it better. sequence model over the history of glance scores would watch the need build up across positions instead of judging each one alone, and backbone fine-tuned to emit dedicated skill-call token would fold the decision into decoding itself. Either leaves the glance and the verdict unchanged, since the gate only decides when they run, and we leave both to future work. Routing behind cloud API. Our experiments run the backbone locally, while many agents call it through hosted API. Gavel moves there by letting the provider host the router. The two projections are trained once per model on corpus of taskskill pairs with contrastive loss, and shipped with the model the way tokenizer is. client uploads its skills, and the provider builds the compressed bank from them in one forward pass each, as it would write prompt cache. On each call the glance runs inside the prefill the provider already performs, reading the hidden states beside the KV cache it keeps for those tokens, and the verdict prefills the shortlisted skills off-path with each skill prefix served from the prompt cache. The response carries the chosen skill, or nothing when the verdict abstains, and the gate runs in the same place from the same states. Nothing crosses the API beyond the skills at installation and the routing decision on each call.
